attributes.translation: I will play once I do my homework.
attributes.nuance_translation: A phrase used specifically to show that (B) only started after (A).

attributes.body:
In order to specifically express that one thing happens/begins to happen after another thing, てから will be used. This expression is regularly translated as 'once (A) happens, (B)', or 'after doing (A), (B)'.

The difference between てから, and the regular て form followed by another verb, is that てから puts more emphasis on the (A) action 'enabling' the (B) action.

Caution

から can come after almost any form of verb. てから is the only form that translates as 'after (A), (B)'. たから, and るから will translate closer to 'because', or 'since'.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: Brief note of て-form with 「から」

attributes.body: て初めて and てから both use the Verb + て form to show actions happening in sequence, but with different nuances. てから simply shows that one event happened after another, while て初めて emphasizes that the second action happened 'only after' or 'not until' meaning 'for the first time after' the previous event.

first_relatable.title: て初めて
first_relatable.meaning: For the first time, Not until, Only after, Only when, Only because

attributes.body: てからというもの can be seen as a more emphatic, formal, and wordy version of てから. Though both mean 'after/once (A), (B)', てから is often used for even simple actions, e.g. 掃除をしてから出掛けます ('I'll go out after I clean up.'), while てからというもの will be used for more profound/meaningful statements, e.g. 娘が生まれてからというもの、人生観が変わった ('Ever since my daughter was born, my view on life changed.').

てから, combining the て form of a verb with から, expresses a sequence of actions, similar to 'A, then B' or 'after A, B' in English (e.g., 食べてから寝る = 'After I eat, I'll sleep'). It can be confused with the past tense た form plus から, which expresses a reason (e.g., 食べたから寝る = 'I ate, so I'll sleep'), focusing on cause rather than sequence.

てから and 上で both convey a sequence of events, but their nuances differ. てから simply indicates that one event follows another. In contrast, 上で emphasizes that the first action or event was a necessary precondition for the second event. Also, 上で is more formal than てから, and often used in business situations or writing.

てから and あとで both convey a sequence of events, but their nuances differ. てから uses the Verb + て form to show that one event follows another. In contrast, あとで follows the past tense (た form) and simply indicates that the second event occurred after the first, without implying any connection between the two.

The Verb + て form is used to connect a verb to another verb, or another part of the sentence. It's commonly used to list actions in sequence, such as 食べて寝る ('I eat, and (then) sleep'). Adding から after the て form emphasizes the sequence, as in 食べてから寝る ('I eat, and (after that) I will sleep').

てから and たら both convey a sequence of events, but their nuances differ. てから simply indicates that one event follows another. In contrast, たら is similar to the English 'when' or 'if' and suggests that the second event is a result of the first. たら can be used in both hypothetical situations ('if A, then B') and past events ('When I did A, B happened').

second_relatable.title: たら
second_relatable.meaning: When, From when, Just when, If
